intro.title: Lists
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Lists are ordered, mutable sequences: `nums = [1, 2, 3]`. Index from 0; negative indices from end.

Methods: append, extend, insert, pop, remove, sort. Lists can hold mixed types.

Lists are workhorses for collections you change often.

intro.title: Indexing and slicing
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Index single elements; slices `start:stop:step` extract subsequences. Slices return new lists for lists; strings stay strings.

Omit start/stop for beginnings/ends. `::-1` reverses.

Out-of-range index raises IndexError; slices clamp gracefully.

intro.title: Tuples
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Tuples are ordered, immutable sequences: `(1, 2)`. Use for fixed records and dict keys.

Packing/unpacking: `a, b = 1, 2`. Parentheses optional for simple tuples.

Immutability protects data you should not change accidentally.

intro.title: Dictionaries
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Dicts map keys to values: `{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}`. Keys must be hashable; lookup is fast.

Methods: keys, values, items, get, pop, update. Dicts preserve insertion order (3.7+).

Use dicts for records, counts, caches, and JSON-like data.

intro.title: Sets
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Sets are unordered collections of unique hashable items: `{1, 2, 3}`.

Use for membership tests, removing duplicates, and set math: union, intersection, difference.

Sets are mutable; frozenset is immutable.

intro.title: The collections module
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The `collections` module has containers made for everyday data jobs. Each one behaves like a dict, list or tuple you already know, with one extra skill.

`Counter` counts things. Give it any list (or string) and it maps each item to how often it appears. `most_common(n)` returns the top `n` as `(item, count)` pairs, and a missing key counts as 0 instead of raising `KeyError`.

```
from collections import Counter

counts = Counter(["apple", "pear", "apple"])
print(counts["apple"], counts["fig"])   # 2 0
print(Counter("banana").most_common(1))   # [('a', 3)]
```

Counters can also do arithmetic: `stock - sold` subtracts the counts and drops every item that reaches zero or less, so `Counter(a=1) - Counter(a=3)` is an empty Counter.

`defaultdict` creates a value the first time you use a missing key. With `defaultdict(list)`, a new key starts as an empty list, so you can group items without first checking `if key not in d`. `defaultdict(set)` collects unique values the same way.

```
from collections import defaultdict

by_letter = defaultdict(list)
for name in ["Ana", "Ben", "Amir"]:
    by_letter[name[0]].append(name)
print(dict(by_letter))   # {'A': ['Ana', 'Amir'], 'B': ['Ben']}
```

`namedtuple` makes a small record type with named fields: after `Product = namedtuple("Product", ["name", "price"])` you can write `p.price` instead of `p[1]`, which makes code much easier to read. It is still a tuple, so it works anywhere a tuple does.

`deque` (say "deck") is a list built for adding and removing at both ends. A list is slow at the front, because every other item has to move along, so a deque is the better choice for a queue. With `maxlen=3` a deque keeps only the last 3 items: appending a fourth drops the oldest. That's exactly what you want for "the latest readings" or a moving window.

`ChainMap(cli, env, defaults)` looks a key up in each dict in turn and returns the first match, so earlier dicts override later ones without copying anything. It's a neat way to layer settings.

Outside `collections`, the `heapq` module finds the largest or smallest items quickly: `heapq.nlargest(3, items, key=...)` returns the top 3, biggest first. And since Python 3.7, a plain `dict` keeps its keys in the order you added them.

intro.title: Choosing a data structure
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Pick list for ordered mutable sequences; tuple for fixed records; dict for key lookup; set for uniqueness and set ops.

Consider ordering, mutability, hashability, memory, and what operations dominate.

Refactoring to the right structure early saves pain in larger programs.
